title: Standard O2C: delivery complete, invoice missing, FI open
prompt: A standard customer order is delivered and PGI is posted. The customer has no invoice, Finance sees COGS but no receivable, and Sales says the order is complete. Diagnose the first broken decision across O2C.
expected_points: Trace sales order → delivery → PGI → billing due state → billing document → FI transfer rather than treating module status independently.
Recognize that PGI can create inventory/COGS impact while Billing/AR remains incomplete.
Check billing relevance, billing block/date/status and document flow before forcing an invoice.
Separate Billing creation from FI transfer and revenue account determination.
Define business completion as consistent delivery, billing, accounting and customer-facing invoice evidence.
follow_up_questions: What if the billing document exists but FI transfer failed?
What if the customer received an e-invoice rejection after FI posting?
red_flags: Says PGI means O2C is complete
Posts AR manually
Creates billing without checking why the item is not due

title: Third-party sales: customer promise versus supplier reality
prompt: A third-party sales order is confirmed to the customer, but the external supplier is late and the customer delivery date is now at risk. Explain the end-to-end ownership and which dates, documents, and integrations you trace before changing the sales order manually.
expected_points: Explain that customer sales demand triggers external procurement rather than own-stock delivery execution.
Trace sales item behavior into purchase requisition/purchase order and supplier confirmation or inbound status.
Compare customer promise with procurement confirmation and the configured third-party process flow.
Keep Sales responsible for customer commitment while Procurement owns supplier execution and confirmation evidence.
Include billing relevance and proof of supplier/customer completion rather than assuming a normal PGI path.
follow_up_questions: How would missing supplier confirmation change ATP or customer communication?
Where would an integration failure between procurement and supplier network appear in the diagnosis?
red_flags: Treats third-party sale as normal warehouse delivery
Changes customer requested date without checking supplier documents
Says Procurement alone owns the customer delay

title: Intercompany: goods shipped, customer invoiced, internal settlement inconsistent
prompt: A selling company invoices the external customer correctly, but the delivering company and intercompany financial flow do not reconcile. Build the cross-company diagnosis without changing the customer invoice first.
expected_points: Separate external customer billing from the intercompany billing/settlement relationship.
Trace delivering plant/company code, sales organization, delivery/PGI, intercompany billing relevance and internal partner data.
Check whether physical delivery and COGS occurred in the delivering company while external revenue/AR belongs to the selling company.
Use document flow and accounting documents for both company-code perspectives before correcting values.
Treat wrong transfer price/accounting and missing intercompany document as different failure classes.
follow_up_questions: What if the external invoice is correct but intercompany billing is not due?
How would transfer-pricing differences affect your ownership model?
red_flags: Cancels the external customer invoice immediately
Treats intercompany as one-company O2C
Looks at only one company code's accounting document

title: Stock transfer: source posted, destination missing stock
prompt: A stock transfer shows the source-side goods issue, but the receiving plant has no expected stock and operations are unsure whether the issue is Inventory Management, EWM, transportation, or integration. Build the diagnosis.
expected_points: Start from the stock-transfer document and identify the exact process variant and movement semantics.
Trace source goods issue, stock-in-transit state where applicable, receiving document/status, destination goods receipt and material documents.
Separate ERP inventory ownership from EWM warehouse execution and TM transport state.
Use quantity/value reconciliation between source, transit and destination before posting a manual correction.
Check asynchronous integration/queue state only after proving which business event is missing.
follow_up_questions: How does a one-step transfer differ from a two-step transfer diagnostically?
What evidence would show EWM executed physically but ERP inventory did not update?
red_flags: Posts a destination GR just to balance stock
Assumes transport completion equals inventory receipt
Looks only at EWM without ERP material-document history

title: Make-to-order: customer demand, production, stock and cost ownership
prompt: A customer-specific product is manufactured, but the finished stock and production cost are not linked to the expected customer requirement. Explain the MTO design and diagnosis across Sales, Production, Inventory and Finance.
expected_points: Identify the sales-order demand and whether the process is truly make-to-order rather than make-to-stock.
Trace requirements into MRP/planned order/production order and the relevant customer-specific account-assignment or stock context.
Check production version/BOM/routing only after demand ownership and order linkage are correct.
Trace component consumption, finished-goods receipt, customer-specific stock/availability and production-order cost receiver/settlement.
Explain how a wrong sales-order/account-assignment link can create technically correct production with the wrong inventory or financial owner.
follow_up_questions: What changes if the business wants anonymous stock before customer allocation?
How would an engineer-to-order scenario extend the object chain?
red_flags: Treats MTO as MTS plus a sales order reference field
Checks production master data before demand ownership
Ignores financial receiver and settlement

title: Subcontracting: components issued, supplier output short
prompt: Components were provided to a subcontractor, but the supplier delivers less finished material than expected and component consumption does not reconcile. Explain the process, stock ownership, and financial checks before adjusting inventory.
expected_points: Start from subcontracting purchasing item behavior and the component requirements linked to the supplier process.
Trace components provided to vendor/special-stock context, supplier receipt of finished material and component consumption at goods receipt or follow-on adjustment.
Reconcile planned versus actual component quantities and remaining special stock at supplier.
Separate physical component variance from purchase-price/invoice and GR/IR effects.
Use controlled subsequent adjustment/reconciliation rather than arbitrary stock correction.
follow_up_questions: What if the subcontractor reports scrap?
How would missing component master/BOM data surface in the process?
red_flags: Writes off component stock immediately
Treats subcontracting as a normal external PO with no component ownership
Ignores supplier special stock and GR/IR

title: Returns and claims: physical return, inspection, credit and stock disagree
prompt: A customer return arrived physically, Quality accepted only part of it, warehouse stock shows a different quantity, and the customer credit is already being requested. Build a controlled returns diagnosis across Sales, QM, Inventory, EWM and Billing.
expected_points: Trace the return reference and reason through returns order, inbound/return delivery and physical receipt.
Separate EWM physical execution from ERP stock state and identify inspection/quality-stock consequences.
Use QM results/usage decision to determine accepted, rejected, blocked or scrapped quantity before final commercial settlement.
Reconcile material documents and stock disposition with the quantity eligible for customer credit.
Keep credit memo/correction as a commercial outcome that should reference the proven physical/quality result, not replace it.
Define completion as consistent return document flow, stock, quality decision, customer credit and FI effect.
follow_up_questions: What if the business wants immediate credit before inspection completes?
How would serial/batch-controlled returns increase the evidence requirement?
red_flags: Credits the full return because the truck arrived
Adjusts warehouse stock to match the requested credit
Treats QM usage decision as unrelated to customer settlement

title: PO change propagation: one saved document, several stale business states
prompt: A buyer changes quantity, delivery date and price on an approved purchase order after the supplier already received the earlier version. An external integration is green, production planning still expects the old date, and an invoice later arrives against the old commercial value. Explain how you control the change end to end.
expected_points: Classify the changed business commitments instead of treating the PO save as process completion.
Check whether the active approval still covers the changed document state and whether supplier communication must be repeated or acknowledged.
Identify every downstream copy or consumer that may hold the old quantity, date or price, including external interfaces and dependent planning.
Separate technical delivery status from business-state reconciliation; a green message does not prove every consumer accepted the intended version.
Trace logistics execution and invoice expectations against the current contract before forcing receipt or invoice corrections.
Close with named ownership for supplier alignment, integration replay where needed, dependent-plan correction, and financial reconciliation.
follow_up_questions: What changes if goods receipt already exists for part of the quantity?
Who should own the final reconciliation when middleware delivered the change but the supplier rejected it?
red_flags: Says the successful PO save completes the change
Treats a green interface as proof of business synchronization
Changes invoice or planning data manually without proving which version each owner accepted

title: Confirmed date: Sales promise disagrees with execution reality
prompt: A sales order has a confirmed delivery date and ATP returned a confirmation, but warehouse and transportation teams say the date cannot be met. The business asks Sales to overwrite the date manually. Diagnose who owns each date and which decision became wrong first.
expected_points: Separate the customer requested date from ATP material confirmation, shipping scheduling, transportation feasibility, and the final customer commitment.
Check confirmed quantity and date in the schedule-line context together with plant and supply source before blaming warehouse execution.
Trace shipping-point, route, loading, picking, transit, calendars, and transportation constraints when supply exists but execution timing does not fit.
Keep Sales or commercial ownership for the customer promise while allowing supply, shipping, warehouse, or transport to own the underlying constraint.
Avoid manual date overwrites until the first wrong decision is proven; recalculate or correct the responsible input instead.
Define proof as a customer-facing promise that is consistent with ATP and downstream execution feasibility.
follow_up_questions: What if ATP confirms the date but the route calendar makes delivery impossible?
What changes when the supply comes from a third-party supplier instead of own stock?
red_flags: Says ATP owns every delivery date
Changes the requested delivery date to make the order look feasible
Says warehouse owns the customer promise

title: GR/IR open: warehouse complete, invoice posted, balance remains
prompt: A purchase order is physically received and the supplier invoice is posted, but GR/IR still has an open balance. Finance asks for a manual clearing entry. Diagnose the process owner and the missing business or value alignment before posting a correction.
expected_points: Start with PO history and reconcile goods-receipt and invoice quantities, values, units, reversals, returns, and open items rather than starting from the G/L balance alone.
Separate physical receipt, invoice verification, valuation, and financial clearing as related but different process states.
Identify whether the mismatch comes from missing receipt or invoice, quantity variance, price/value variance, reversal, return, or incomplete closure.
Assign correction to the owner of the missing or wrong business event instead of treating every GR/IR balance as Finance housekeeping.
Avoid an unexplained manual journal entry that clears FI while leaving procurement history inconsistent.
Close with controlled correction or reversal and proof that PO history, quantities, values, and financial state reconcile.
follow_up_questions: How does the diagnosis change when the invoice arrives before goods receipt?
What if quantities match but the remaining difference is value-related?
red_flags: Says Finance owns GR/IR because it is a G/L account
Clears the balance manually before checking PO history
Checks only invoice accounting and ignores receipt reversals or returns

title: Account assignment: PO posts correctly to the wrong business owner
prompt: A consumable or service purchase order posts without a technical error, but the cost lands on the wrong cost center, internal order, project, or other receiver. The buyer asks Finance to change the G/L account. Explain where cost ownership should be decided and how you prevent the problem from repeating.
expected_points: Start with the business receiver: who should economically own the purchase and why.
Then validate account-assignment category and the concrete receiver object before moving to G/L or FI/CO account determination.
Separate manually entered values, defaults, master-data or organizational derivation, configuration, workflow, and integration inputs as possible causes.
Distinguish a one-time incorrect document from a repeated design problem in defaults, governance, or process ownership.
If posting already occurred, preserve auditability through the correct reversal, reposting, settlement, or controlled correction path rather than hiding the original state.
Prevent recurrence by placing validation and default ownership at the layer that knows the business receiver, not by hardcoding one account in downstream code.
follow_up_questions: How would multiple account assignment change your control model?
What if the account-assignment receiver is correct but the G/L account is wrong?
red_flags: Changes only the G/L account
Calls it an FI problem because the posting is wrong
Hardcodes a cost center or account without naming the business owner

title: Master-data validation: green replication, broken sales execution
prompt: A material is created in the governed source and replicates successfully to SAP S/4HANA. The interface is green, but a sales order later cannot continue because a business-critical logistics attribute is missing. Integration proposes making the field mandatory in middleware. Decide where the validation should live and how you correct already distributed data.
expected_points: Separate enterprise master-data quality, transaction-specific protection, and interface-contract validation instead of solving every missing field in middleware.
If the attribute is globally required for the governed material state, place the primary rule in MDG or the authoritative master-data governance layer so the defect is prevented before distribution.
If the rule is valid only for one process context, keep the protection close to the consuming application or transaction instead of redefining the enterprise master-data contract.
Use integration validation for schema, mandatory contract fields, identifiers, versions, and receiver prerequisites, but do not turn integration into a parallel stewardship system.
Identify the authoritative source and correction owner, then replicate or reconcile corrected records to consumers that already received the bad state.
Define completion as governed data corrected, distribution reconciled, and the target business process proven usable without local manual repair.
follow_up_questions: What changes if only one country or sales organization requires the field?
What if the target system has a stricter contract than the enterprise master-data model?
red_flags: Makes every downstream field mandatory in middleware
Says a green replication proves master-data quality
Fixes the material only in the consuming system without correcting the authoritative source

title: AI agent authority: can act does not mean should act
prompt: An AI agent investigates a delayed customer order. It can read order and interface evidence and has tools that could change a confirmed date, replay an IDoc, and release a business block. The agent is confident it knows the cause. Define which actions it may take autonomously and where accountable human or deterministic controls must remain in the loop.
expected_points: Separate retrieval, summarization, classification, proposal, and execution as different autonomy levels instead of treating tool access as one permission.
Allow low-risk evidence work first and require stronger gates as actions affect customer commitments, inventory, money, compliance, or other consequential business state.
Keep business-control authority with the authorised process owner for decisions such as credit or compliance release; the agent may collect evidence and prepare a recommendation.

For bounded technical actions such as replay, require deterministic preconditions, least-privilege execution identity, duplicate/idempotency checks, audit evidence, and post-action business reconciliation.
Do not let model confidence replace authorization. The tool identity, allowed scope, approval path, and recovery owner must be explicit outside the model.
Verify the resulting SAP business state after any action; a successful tool or API response is not proof that the logistics process is complete.
follow_up_questions: Would you allow autonomous IDoc replay if the receiver is idempotent and the target document does not exist?
What extra control would you require before an agent changes a customer-confirmed date?
red_flags: Lets the agent execute because confidence is high
Uses one broad technical user for every SAP action
Treats a successful API response as business completion
